extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemakers, agency counsel, policy makers, and practitioners handling notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for assessing, deterring, and handling malattributed and computer-generated comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, including criminal statutes, APA constraints, policy tradeoffs, technological mitigations, and harms to individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making False Statements (18 U.S.C. § 1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on making “false, fictitious, or fraudulent” statements to a federal agency under 18 U.S.C. § 1001; unlike fraud it does not require financial or property loss to the government or reliance by the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements discussed: (1) a false or fictitious statement or representation (malattributed comment asserting another as submitter qualifies); (2) knowing or willful falsehood (the programmer/authorizing actor knows misidentifications occur); (3) a matter within the agency's jurisdiction (a notice-and-comment rulemaking qualifies); and (4) materiality—the statement must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the decisionmaking body (Neder v. United States). Use of a false name is not automatically material unless the identity (or claimed identity/authority) would affect the weight given to the comment. Example: a comment falsely claiming to be submitted by an expert or affected party could be material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality of a False Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiality requires that the false statement “has a natural tendency to influence, or [is] capable of influencing, the decision of the decisionmaking body to which it was addressed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere false name is immaterial where the agency only cares about comment content; a false claim of expertise, unique experience, or status (Ph.D., long-time employee, affected property owner) is more likely to be material because it changes the weight of the comment. Assess whether the misstatement communicates background that would influence agency evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Fraud-Based Criminal Prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud-based crimes typically require showing substantial harm to the government (e.g., financial/property loss or reliance), which may be difficult in the context of malattributed comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the difficulty of showing substantial harm, prosecutors may be disinclined to pursue fraud charges; in many contexts the more plausible charging theory might be conspiracy rather than fraud, but conspiratorial elements are different and must be proven separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Malattribution is a 'Material' Falsehood (bespoke/expert impersonation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A malattributed comment that falsely claims to be from someone with extensive relevant expertise or a particular stake (e.g., a Ph.D. researcher, long-time employee, product user, property owner) can be material because the claimed background would give the comment more weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if only conveyed through a name, if that name communicates the relevant background, the falsehood may be material under § 1001. Agencies should be alert to bespoke comments that purport to come from authoritative sources and verify provenance where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA Requirement to Accept and Consider Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 553) agencies must provide notice and an opportunity to comment and must consider the relevant matter presented; courts require agencies to respond to significant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty arguably extends to malattributed comments insofar as they raise important or substantive points; agencies cannot simply refuse to accept all malattributed comments absent a clear, published policy. However, agencies commonly conclude many comments do not require individualized responses and may treat malattribution as a factor in deeming a comment insubstantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Authority to Impose Reasonable Form and Content Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are free to impose reasonable requirements on the form and content of public comments (e.g., deadlines, civility, not revealing confidential information) and many agencies adopt policies about anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may prohibit anonymous comments or set other participation rules and publish clear policies. Prior ACUS recommendations urge agencies to adopt and publish policies regarding anonymous submissions—by analogy agencies can set policies regarding malattributed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation (or Not) to 'Cleanse' the Docket of Malattributed Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists whether the APA requires agencies to remove malattributed comments from the docket or whether agencies may simply ignore noncontributory submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purging dockets imposes costs and may impede judicial review of the full record; to justify purging, malattributed comments must cause affirmative harm beyond being merely useless (e.g., drowning out legitimate comments or misleading other stakeholders). The strongest case for removal is a sophisticated bespoke 'deep fake' that deceives the agency or other commenters; routine duplicative or generic malattributed comments are less likely to warrant removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Reliance on Malattributed Comments and 'Reasoned Decisionmaking'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it violates the APA for an agency to read or rely on a comment submitted under a false name depends on the arbitrary-and-capricious standard requiring reasoned decisionmaking (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be arbitrary and capricious to rely on malattributed comments as a measure of public sentiment or to treat an impersonated authority as an expert; but if a comment is relevant, factually accurate, and informative, an agency may use it even if the name is false. There is no per se rule requiring or forbidding reliance; determinations are case-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of Misleading the Agency about Commenter Identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can mislead agencies about who submitted a comment—particularly when a recognizable or authoritative name is used or when the comment asserts particular personal experience or situated knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large-scale identical submissions agencies often do not notice names; recognizable names (or claims of particular experience) pose greater risk of misleading because the agency might give extra weight. Agencies should be aware that detection is easier when the purported author is well-known to agency staff; for lesser-known names, provenance checks may be necessary where weight hinges on identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of Misleading about Public Sentiment (mass/computer-generated comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments—often a form of computer-generated mass comments—can create the appearance of widespread public support or opposition when that is not the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal concern with mass malattributed comments is that agencies may infer broader public sentiment from large numbers of near-identical submissions bearing different (real or fake) names. The malattribution itself is less important than the fact that many submissions are from a single source. Agencies should consider how they weight volume of comments and whether safeguards (e.g., identifying verified mass campaign submissions) are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms to Individuals Whose Names Are Used
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can cause psychological and reputational harms to the people whose names and email addresses are used without permission, even if they never become aware or suffer financial loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible harms include annoyance, distress, reputational injury if a comment becomes publicly visible and reflects poorly on the ostensible author, and concerns resembling identity theft. Agencies should consider notification or removal procedures when individuals complain, and recognize that quantifying harms may be difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discouraging Malattributed Comments through User Notices and Legal Warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov and e-rulemaking systems can and do include user notices that encourage commenters to submit their own comments and warn that knowingly making materially false statements about identity can violate federal law (citing 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and § 1028).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Click-to-verify language is used to deter malattribution but may have limited impact on large-scale operations. Placement, visibility, and clarity of notices matter; notices may also support later enforcement or administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Policies and Protocols for Handling Suspected Malattributed Comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies need protocols to address whether and how to resolve questions about a comment’s provenance, whether to flag potential malattributions, and how to assist investigations or prosecutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions include whether to expend resources verifying authorship vs. simply flagging suspect comments, when to refer potential criminal violations to law enforcement, and how to staff responses. Agencies should consider published policies to provide transparency about how malattributed comments will be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological Authentication Options
rubrics_metrics.description: Various technologies exist to authenticate users (secure login, two-factor authentication, biometrics, security questions, database verification, explicit additional acknowledgments), but agencies generally lack the identity-authentication systems used for driver’s licenses or commercial transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentication techniques can reduce malattributed and automated submissions but conflict with policies permitting anonymous comments and may raise access and privacy concerns. Agencies should weigh tradeoffs, adopt targeted authentication where appropriate (e.g., for verified mass filers), and consider the burden on participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CAPTCHA / reCAPTCHA and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA are used to ensure comment submitters are human and serve as a 'speed bump' against bots; reCAPTCHA v3 uses risk analysis to assign scores without human interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAPTCHA historically deterred automated attacks but tools to defeat it exist; reCAPTCHA v3's risk scoring can alert administrators to fraudulent activity but is not foolproof. Such tools help reduce computer-generated comments and may incidentally reduce malattribution but will not stop determined large-scale campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations.gov API and Verified Mass-Comment Posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov provides a comment API that allows authorized entities to post mass comment campaigns if verified by GSA using a commercial identity validation service; the service aims to assure that organizations are 'who they say they are' but does not verify individual commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism supports legitimate organized campaigns while providing a verification trail for mass filers, but it does not eliminate risks from individual malattributed submissions. Agencies can require or encourage use of verified channels for large campaigns to improve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs Between Authentication and Anonymous Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentication to verify commenter identity is technically feasible but runs into tension with agency policies that permit anonymous comments and with concerns about access to participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must balance deterrence of abuse against protecting participation and anonymity. Policies can be tailored—e.g., requiring verification for certain submission channels, offering anonymous submission with caveats about weight given, or providing clear published rules about how anonymous and verified comments will be treated.
